say: A standard operating procedure, or SOP, is the written way your workroom handles every order, on one page on the wall.
Stage one, intake. Style agreed, fabric checked, deposit paid, due date set.

panel.heading: Six stages, six owners
items: Intake: style, measurements, deposit, due date
Cut: pieces cut, notched, bundled with ticket
Sew: operations done in order
Finish: hand work, buttons, pressing
Inspect: against the golden sample
Deliver: balance paid, ticket closed

say: Stage two, cut. The pieces are cut and bundled with a job ticket that travels with the garment to delivery.

say: Put each order on a card on a job board, one column per stage, and set a limit, for example no more than 8 garments in Sew. When the column is full, the cutter helps finish instead.

say: Little's law says average lead time equals work in progress divided by garments finished per day.

panel.heading: Why clients wait 9 days
items: Lead time = work in progress ÷ daily throughput
Adaeze: 36 garments ÷ 4 a day = 9 days
Cap work in progress at 20: about 5 days
Set due dates from your board, not from hope

say: Adaeze had about 36 garments inside, and finished 4 a day. 36 divided by 4 is 9 working days.

say: By not cutting new work until the Sew column dropped, she capped it at 20. Now each garment spends about 5 days inside, at no extra cost.

say: Checking only at the end catches faults when they cost most to fix. So check at four gates. At intake, look along the fabric in daylight for holes and shading.

panel.heading: Four checks along the line
items: Fabric and trims check at intake
Cut check before sewing
First-piece check for each operation
Final inspection before the press

say: Before sewing, count the pieces and check the measurement card. A cutting error found here costs minutes, not the fabric.

say: Adaeze inspected 180 garments in a month and 27 had a fault. That is a defect rate of 15%.
She sorted the faults from most to least. Uneven hems came first, 9 of the 27.

panel.heading: Fix the vital few faults first

cards.d: 33.3% of faults. Adaeze retrains one machinist on levelling hems.
Now 59.3% together. She adds a first-piece check for zips.
Now 77.8% together. The cut check gets a second look at the measurement card.

say: A growing workroom has more machines and cables. Spread heavy loads, switch off at the wall, keep an extinguisher for electrical fires by a clear exit, and stand irons on their heel.
Protect clients too. Lock away measurement books and never post a client's photo without her permission.

panel.heading: Write these into your SOP
items: Do not overload extension boxes
Switch off at the wall at closing
Extinguisher for electrical fires, exits clear
Irons on their heel, cords off walkways
Measurement books locked away
No client photo posted without permission

say: To remember. Use a one-page SOP, job tickets and a work in progress limit. Check at four gates and log every fault. Cost by the minute.
Treat any plan above about 85 to 90% of your productive minutes as a warning.

panel.heading: Remember
items: One-page SOP, job tickets and a WIP limit
Lead time = work in progress ÷ throughput
Four quality gates and a defect log
Price = total cost ÷ (1 − margin)
Plans above 85 to 90% of capacity are a warning
